note.note:
H&P – Super Detailed

Consult Summary:
19-year-old female university student presents with 6–7 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, suprapubic ache, and new pink-tinged urine; clinical picture most consistent with an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Burning/stinging on urination with markedly increased urinary frequency; began just under one week ago.  
• Progression: Persistent over the week; today for the first time noted pink-tinged urine.  
• Pain description: Dull/aching suprapubic discomfort, worse while voiding; does not radiate to back or sides.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, flank/back pain. No abnormal vaginal discharge. Bowels unchanged from baseline IBS.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: None stated; not cramp-like; no clear triggers identified.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives/positives):  
  – GU: Dysuria, frequency, micro-hematuria; no flank pain, no vaginal discharge.  
  – GI: Baseline variable bowel habit from IBS; no new abdominal symptoms.  
  – Constitutional: No subjective fever or malaise.  
  – Others: No nausea, vomiting, respiratory or neurologic complaints reported.

Past Medical History:
• Irritable Bowel Syndrome – variable stool frequency/consistency; uses mebeverine for cramps.  
• No prior urinary or renal disease reported.

Medications:
• Combined oral contraceptive pill – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Mebeverine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• Clindamycin – previous adverse reaction (details not provided).

Social History:
• Lives in university halls with a flatmate; first-year English student.  
• Sexually active with long-term boyfriend; typically does not use condoms. Last unprotected intercourse ≈1 week ago.  
• Alcohol: Occasional social drinking.  
• Tobacco: Non-smoker.  
• Recreational drugs: Tried cannabis once 1½ weeks ago; no ongoing use.  
• Last menstrual period: 2 weeks ago; on combined pill.

Family History:
• No known kidney or bladder disease; otherwise non-contributory.

Physical Examination:
• Telehealth visit – no vitals or physical exam performed.  
• Patient denies fever.

Investigations:
• None completed to date. Plan to obtain mid-stream urine for dipstick, microscopy, culture & sensitivity.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Suspected acute uncomplicated cystitis (bacterial UTI)  
  • Assessment: Classic triad of dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain in healthy young woman; mild micro-hematuria today; no systemic or upper-tract features.  
  • Plan:  
    – Start empiric oral antibiotic: Trimethoprim OR Nitrofurantoin (3-day course); medication, dose, and final choice to be confirmed once prescription issued.  
    – Provide urine pot and arrange drop-off at practice for dipstick + culture.  
    – Hydration advice: Increase oral fluids.  
    – Analgesia: Paracetamol as needed (dose not documented).  
    – Safety-netting: Return sooner for fever, flank/back pain, vomiting, or worsening symptoms; routine follow-up if no improvement within one week.  
    – Review culture results and adjust antibiotics if resistance noted.

Issue 2 – Irritable Bowel Syndrome (stable)  
  • Assessment: Baseline variability; no acute change.  
  • Plan: Continue current mebeverine.

Issue 3 – Health promotion / substance use  
  • Assessment: Single recent cannabis use.  
  • Plan: Counseling provided to avoid future cannabis use; reinforce moderation with alcohol.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute uncomplicated cystitis – High likelihood: Fits dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, mild hematuria, absence of systemic signs.  
2. Chlamydial/gonococcal urethritis or cervicitis – Moderate likelihood: Recent unprotected sex could mimic cystitis; lack of vaginal discharge and pelvic pain makes less likely but consider STI screening if symptoms persist or recur.  
3. Distal ureteric/bladder stone – Low likelihood: Hematuria possible, but absence of colicky flank pain and young age make this less probable.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing but expected: Objective vitals, abdominal/genitourinary exam, full medication doses/routes, surgical history, immunization status.  
• Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Clear for most parts; minor conversational fillers, no significant inaudible sections.
